statement: The first surviving photograph was taken in 1826 or 1827.
explanation: Joseph Nicéphore Niépce created 'View from the Window at Le Gras' using a pewter plate coated with bitumen. It required an exposure of several hours.

statement: The word 'photography' means 'drawing with light'.
explanation: The word is derived from the Greek 'phōs' (light) and 'graphé' (drawing or writing), literally meaning 'drawing with light'.

statement: Kodak invented the first digital camera.
explanation: In 1975, Kodak engineer Steve Sasson built the first self-contained digital camera, which captured a 0.01-megapixel image onto a cassette tape.

statement: Megapixels are the most important factor in image quality.
explanation: Sensor size, dynamic range, lens quality, and image processing are equally or more important than pixel count alone.

statement: The most viewed photograph in history is the Windows XP default wallpaper.
explanation: 'Bliss', photographed by Charles O'Rear in Sonoma County, California in 1996, was seen by billions of Windows XP users worldwide.

statement: Smiling in early photographs was common practice.
explanation: Early photographic exposures required subjects to remain still for minutes. Holding a smile for that long was impractical, and formal painted portraiture norms also discouraged smiling.

statement: The first color photograph was taken in 1861.
explanation: Physicist James Clerk Maxwell demonstrated the first color photograph — an image of a tartan ribbon taken by Thomas Sutton — at the Royal Institution of Great Britain.

statement: A larger f-number on a lens means a larger aperture opening.
explanation: The f-number is a fraction of focal length divided by aperture diameter. A larger f-number (e.g., f/16) means a smaller physical opening, and vice versa.

statement: The first known photographic self-portrait was taken in 1839.
explanation: Robert Cornelius, a chemist and photographer from Philadelphia, took a daguerreotype of himself in October 1839, making it one of the earliest known photographs of a person.

statement: Red-eye in photographs is caused by camera flash reflecting off blood vessels.
explanation: The flash illuminates the blood-rich retina at the back of the eye. The red light reflects back through the dilated pupil and is captured by the camera sensor.

statement: Polaroid introduced the world's first commercially available instant camera.
explanation: Edwin Land's Polaroid Land Camera Model 95, launched in 1948, was the first commercially available instant camera and sold out on its first day.

statement: A camera's shutter speed controls the depth of field.
explanation: Depth of field is primarily controlled by aperture. A wider aperture produces a shallower depth of field. Shutter speed controls motion blur and exposure time.

statement: ISO measures a camera sensor's (or film's) sensitivity to light.
explanation: ISO stands for International Organization for Standardization. A higher ISO value means greater sensitivity to light, which is useful in low-light conditions but introduces more noise.

statement: The Rule of Thirds is the definitive law of photographic composition.
explanation: The Rule of Thirds is a widely taught guideline, not a rule. Many iconic and award-winning photographs deliberately break it for artistic effect.

statement: Camera lenses are constructed from multiple glass elements.
explanation: Modern lenses use multiple glass elements arranged in groups. Each element is shaped and coated to correct optical aberrations like chromatic distortion and vignetting.

statement: Humanity now takes more photos every two minutes than were taken in all of the 1800s.
explanation: With smartphone cameras and social media, over 1.4 trillion photos are taken each year. The total photographs taken in the entire 19th century is estimated in the millions.

statement: The first digital camera had a megapixel sensor.
explanation: Steve Sasson's 1975 prototype Kodak camera produced a 0.01-megapixel (100×100 pixel) black-and-white image stored on a digital cassette tape.

statement: Exposure compensation adjusts the brightness of an image.
explanation: Exposure compensation (+/-) allows photographers to intentionally over or underexpose an image relative to what the camera's metering system recommends.

statement: The daguerreotype process produced images on glass plates.
explanation: Daguerreotypes were produced on silver-coated copper plates that had been exposed to iodine vapour. Glass plates were used by later processes like the wet collodion process.

statement: A mirrorless camera has no reflex mirror inside the body.
explanation: Unlike a DSLR, a mirrorless camera removes the reflex mirror and optical viewfinder, using instead a digital sensor for both image capture and live preview.

statement: RAW image files contain processed, compressed image data.
explanation: RAW files contain minimally processed, uncompressed (or losslessly compressed) data directly from the camera sensor, giving photographers maximum flexibility in post-processing.

statement: Long exposure photography can make moving water appear silky and smooth.
explanation: Using a slow shutter speed (typically 0.5 seconds or longer) blurs the motion of flowing water, creating a smooth, mist-like effect.

statement: Henri Cartier-Bresson coined the term 'the decisive moment'.
explanation: French photographer Henri Cartier-Bresson used this concept to describe the precise instant when all visual and emotional elements of a scene align perfectly in a single frame.

statement: White balance has no effect on RAW files.
explanation: While white balance can be fully corrected in post-processing for RAW files, the camera still embeds a white balance setting in the metadata that affects the preview.

statement: Ansel Adams developed the Zone System for controlling exposure and development.
explanation: Ansel Adams and Fred Archer developed the Zone System in 1940 to give photographers precise control over exposure and development to achieve a desired tonal range.

statement: The principle behind the camera obscura was described centuries before photography existed.
explanation: Scholars such as Mozi in China and Alhazen in the Arab world described how light passing through a small hole projects an inverted image.

statement: Louis Daguerre's photographic process was publicly announced in 1839.
explanation: The French government bought the rights and gave the daguerreotype to the world 'free to all' in August 1839.

statement: William Henry Fox Talbot invented a negative-to-positive photographic process.
explanation: His calotype process allowed many prints to be made from a single paper negative, a foundation of photography for over a century.

statement: George Eastman launched the Kodak camera in 1888 with the slogan 'You press the button, we do the rest'.
explanation: The pre-loaded camera was returned to Kodak for developing, putting photography within reach of ordinary people.

statement: Eadweard Muybridge used photographs to show that a galloping horse has all four hooves off the ground at once.
explanation: His 1870s experiments used a row of cameras triggered by tripwires to capture the horse in sequential frames.

statement: Dorothea Lange took the famous 'Migrant Mother' photograph in 1936.
explanation: The image of Florence Owens Thompson became an icon of the Great Depression.

statement: Apollo astronauts used Hasselblad cameras on the Moon.
explanation: Most of the cameras were left behind on the lunar surface, and only the film magazines came back to Earth.

statement: The 'Earthrise' photograph was taken by astronaut Bill Anders during Apollo 8.
explanation: Taken in December 1968, it showed Earth rising above the lunar horizon and became one of the most influential images in history.

statement: A slower shutter speed produces more motion blur.
explanation: The shutter stays open longer, so anything moving during the exposure is recorded as a streak.

statement: Aperture size controls how much of an image appears in focus.
explanation: A wide aperture gives a shallow depth of field with a blurred background, while a narrow aperture keeps more of the scene sharp.

statement: 'Golden hour' refers to the soft, warm light shortly after sunrise and before sunset.
explanation: The Sun is low in the sky, so its light passes through more atmosphere, giving it a warmer and softer look.

statement: The photography term 'bokeh' comes from a Japanese word.
explanation: It comes from 'boke', meaning blur or haze, and describes the aesthetic quality of out-of-focus areas of a photo.

statement: A full-frame camera sensor is about the same size as a frame of 35mm film.
explanation: A full-frame sensor measures roughly 36 × 24 mm, matching the traditional 35mm film frame.

statement: A prime lens has a fixed focal length.
explanation: Unlike a zoom lens, a prime lens cannot change its focal length, which often lets it have a wider aperture and sharper images.

statement: A histogram shows how the tones in a photo are distributed from dark to bright.
explanation: Photographers use it to check for under- and overexposure, particularly when the screen is hard to see.

statement: A polarising filter can reduce reflections from water and glass.
explanation: It blocks light waves vibrating in certain directions, which also deepens the blue of the sky.

statement: A neutral density (ND) filter reduces the amount of light entering the lens without changing colours.
explanation: It lets photographers use slow shutter speeds or wide apertures in bright conditions.

statement: The Leica I, released in 1925, helped popularise 35mm film photography.
explanation: Designed by Oskar Barnack, it showed that a small, portable camera could produce high-quality negatives.

statement: A pinhole camera has no lens.
explanation: A tiny hole lets light into a dark box and forms an inverted image on the film or sensor.

statement: Ansel Adams was a founding member of Group f/64.
explanation: The group, formed in 1932, championed sharply focused 'straight' photography using very small apertures.

statement: Steve McCurry photographed the 'Afghan Girl' for National Geographic in 1984.
explanation: The photo, of a young girl in a refugee camp in Pakistan, appeared on the magazine's cover in June 1985.

statement: A cyanotype produces a blue-toned print.
explanation: Invented by John Herschel in 1842, the process uses iron salts, which turn a deep Prussian blue when exposed to UV light.

statement: Each full stop of exposure doubles or halves the amount of light.
explanation: Opening the aperture by one stop, or halving the shutter speed, changes the light reaching the sensor by a factor of two.

statement: DSLR stands for digital single-lens reflex.
explanation: A mirror inside the camera reflects light up to the optical viewfinder until the shutter fires.

statement: Most digital camera sensors use a Bayer filter with twice as many green filters as red or blue.
explanation: This pattern mimics the human eye's greater sensitivity to green light, and software then reconstructs full colour for every pixel.

statement: JPEG is a lossy format.
explanation: JPEG discards some image data to reduce file size, and quality drops a little each time a file is re-saved.

statement: A RAW file keeps more image data than a JPEG.
explanation: Because RAW files store the sensor's original data, they allow more flexibility when adjusting exposure and colour.

statement: The 'Sunny 16' rule is a way to estimate exposure without a light meter.
explanation: On a bright, sunny day, set the aperture to f/16 and the shutter speed to the reciprocal of the ISO.

statement: Aperture, shutter speed and ISO make up the exposure triangle.
explanation: Changing one of them affects the others if you want to keep the same overall brightness.

statement: Raising the ISO generally makes a photo noisier.
explanation: A higher ISO amplifies the sensor's signal, which also amplifies random noise, so images look grainier.

statement: The first photograph to include a person was taken by Louis Daguerre in Paris in 1838.
explanation: Because of the long exposure, only a man having his boots polished stood still long enough to appear on the street.

statement: Vivian Maier's street photographs were only discovered after her death.
explanation: Her work was found in an auction storage locker in 2007 and has since been recognised among the best street photography of the 20th century.

statement: Infrared photography can make green foliage look white.
explanation: Leaves reflect a lot of infrared light, known as the Wood effect, so they appear pale or glowing in infrared images.

statement: The famous 1934 'Surgeon's Photograph' of the Loch Ness Monster was a hoax.
explanation: It turned out to be a toy submarine with a sculpted head, as confessed decades later.

statement: The Cottingley Fairies photographs were faked by two young cousins.
explanation: The 1917 photos, made with paper cut-outs, famously fooled Sir Arthur Conan Doyle.

statement: Instagram began as a location check-in app called Burbn.
explanation: Its founders noticed that users liked the photo features most and refocused the app around them before launching Instagram in 2010.

statement: Kodak filed for bankruptcy protection in 2012.
explanation: The company that had dominated film photography struggled to adapt to the shift to digital imaging.

statement: The Voyager 1 'Pale Blue Dot' photograph shows Earth as a tiny speck from about 6 billion kilometres away.
explanation: Taken in 1990 at Carl Sagan's request, it shows Earth as less than a pixel in size.

statement: A higher ISO always produces better image quality.
explanation: Higher ISO increases sensitivity but also adds noise, so photographers use the lowest ISO that still gives a proper exposure.

statement: You should never use flash outdoors.
explanation: Fill flash can lighten harsh shadows on faces in bright sunlight and is often used by professionals.

statement: Overcast days are bad for photography.
explanation: Clouds act as a giant softbox, spreading light evenly, which is flattering for portraits and rich colours.

statement: Midday is the best time to photograph portraits outdoors.
explanation: The overhead Sun creates harsh shadows under the eyes and nose, so softer morning or evening light is usually preferred.

statement: A lens's focal length is the physical length of the lens barrel.
explanation: Focal length is the distance from the optical centre of the lens to the sensor when focused at infinity, and is not the lens's physical length.

statement: JPEG files give more editing flexibility than RAW files.
explanation: RAW files keep far more tonal and colour information, so they can handle larger adjustments without degrading.

statement: A faster shutter speed lets more light into the camera.
explanation: A faster shutter is open for less time, so less light reaches the sensor.

statement: More expensive cameras always take better photographs.
explanation: Composition, lighting and timing matter more than equipment, and many classic images were taken with simple cameras.

statement: Digital zoom captures more detail than optical zoom.
explanation: Digital zoom simply crops and enlarges the image, whereas optical zoom changes the lens to gather real detail.

statement: Film photography stopped completely once digital cameras arrived.
explanation: Film is still manufactured and has seen a revival among photographers who enjoy its look and process.

statement: Adobe built the first version of Photoshop from scratch.
explanation: Photoshop was originally written by brothers Thomas and John Knoll, and Adobe licensed it in 1988 before buying it.

statement: Leica invented the camera.
explanation: Cameras existed in the 1800s long before Leica, which made its mark with the compact 35mm camera in the 1920s.

statement: The first photograph ever taken was a portrait.
explanation: The earliest surviving photograph shows the view from a window of Niépce's estate in France.

statement: A UV filter always improves image quality.
explanation: Modern lenses already have UV-blocking coatings, and an extra piece of glass can add flare or reduce sharpness.

statement: Image stabilisation freezes motion of the subject.
explanation: Stabilisation only compensates for camera shake and can't stop a moving subject from blurring.

statement: A full-frame camera always has more megapixels than a smaller-sensor camera.
explanation: Sensor size and megapixel count are independent, and some smaller-sensor cameras have more megapixels than full-frame ones.

statement: Polaroid pictures develop faster if you shake them.
explanation: Shaking has no real effect and could even damage the image as the chemicals develop.

statement: The camera never lies.
explanation: Framing, lenses, lighting, timing and editing can all change what a photograph appears to show.

statement: Bulb mode limits exposures to a maximum of 30 seconds.
explanation: In bulb mode, the shutter stays open for as long as the button is held, which makes it useful for long night-time exposures.

statement: Mirrorless cameras don't have a viewfinder.
explanation: Many mirrorless cameras have an electronic viewfinder that shows a live digital preview.

statement: A camera records scenes exactly the way the human eye sees them.
explanation: Cameras have different dynamic range, perspective, and colour response from the human eye and brain.

statement: A daguerreotype could be copied easily from a negative.
explanation: Daguerreotypes were unique positive images on metal and could not be reproduced from a negative.

statement: Ansel Adams is best known for his colour photography.
explanation: Adams is famous for black-and-white landscapes, such as those of Yosemite and the American West.

statement: The memory card you use determines your image quality.
explanation: A memory card only stores files; image quality depends on the sensor, lens and settings.

statement: Lens hoods are only for keeping rain off the lens.
explanation: A hood blocks stray light to reduce flare and improve contrast, and also protects the front of the lens.

statement: Digital photographs will last forever without any effort.
explanation: Files can be lost to drive failure, corruption or obsolete formats, so backups and migration are needed.

statement: Louis Daguerre invented photography single-handedly.
explanation: Nicéphore Niépce made the first photograph, Daguerre refined the process after working with him, and Talbot developed a rival process.

statement: Shutter speed determines how sharp a lens is.
explanation: Shutter speed affects motion blur and exposure, while sharpness depends on the lens, aperture, focus and stability.

statement: Taking a photo with a flash will always freeze any motion in the scene.
explanation: Ambient light can still register during a long exposure, causing ghosting blur even though the flash froze part of the action.

statement: Black-and-white photography means that the camera cannot record colour.
explanation: Digital cameras record colour data, and black-and-white images are usually made by converting to monochrome afterwards.

statement: A wider lens always makes a person look slimmer.
explanation: Wide-angle lenses close to a subject can distort and exaggerate features, particularly at the edges of the frame.

statement: Shooting at higher resolutions guarantees sharper photos.
explanation: Poor focus, camera shake or a weak lens will still produce soft images, no matter the pixel count.

statement: Panning with a slow shutter speed can keep a moving subject sharp while blurring the background.
explanation: Following the subject smoothly during the exposure makes it appear still relative to the camera, while the background smears into streaks.

statement: Adobe Photoshop 1.0 was released in 1990.
explanation: The first version ran only on Macintosh computers and has since become a shorthand for image editing.

statement: Magnum Photos was founded in 1947 by photographers including Robert Capa and Henri Cartier-Bresson.
explanation: The cooperative gave photographers control over their own work and became one of the most famous photo agencies.

statement: The 'Blue Marble' photograph of the whole Earth was taken by the Apollo 17 crew in 1972.
explanation: It is one of the most widely reproduced images in history and shows Earth fully lit by the Sun.

statement: A telephoto lens changes the perspective of a scene no matter where you stand.
explanation: Perspective depends on the camera's position relative to the subject, whereas a telephoto lens only magnifies and crops the view.
